proposal.reason: Trial 1 with word features and C=0.3 collapsed to majority-class behavior: macro_f1 0.4630 and class_recall [1.0, 0.0], so spam was never recalled. A character n-gram representation with higher regularization strength is a reasonable next primary-split probe because it changes the feature space and capacity while staying within the registered logistic single-text route.
proposal.review: The only completed primary trial is single_word_C0.3. Its train/search gap is small, but the zero spam recall indicates the fitted decision rule is not useful for the spam class under that configuration. This is evidence for changing representation/capacity, not proof that char features will fix the issue. No confirmation-split measurements are available or compared.
proposal.hypothesis: Character n-grams with C=3.0 may capture spam-indicative substrings and punctuation patterns that word-level C=0.3 did not exploit, potentially increasing spam recall and macro_f1 relative to the majority-class collapse in trial 1.
proposal.uncertainty: The direction and magnitude of macro_f1 change are unknown. The prior collapse may persist if class imbalance dominates, and higher C could overfit or still predict mostly ham. This candidate is selected as a primary-split probe, not as a verified improvement.

proposal.reason: Trial 2 with char features and C=3.0 reached macro_f1 0.9257 and nonzero spam recall, while trial 1 with word features and C=0.3 collapsed to majority-class behavior. A word+char representation at C=3.0 is a reasonable primary-split probe because it keeps the capacity that worked for char features while adding word-token information that may capture complementary spam cues.
proposal.review: The completed primary evidence is limited to two trials. Trial 1 shows word-only C=0.3 was not useful for spam recall. Trial 2 shows char-only C=3.0 was much stronger, but its train/search gap was 0.0541 and spam recall was 0.7692, so it is not proof of a robust solution. No confirmation-split measurements are available or compared.
proposal.hypothesis: Combining word and character n-gram features at C=3.0 may capture both token-level and substring-level spam indicators, potentially improving macro_f1 or spam recall relative to char-only C=3.0, but the direction and magnitude are unknown.
proposal.uncertainty: The combined representation may overfit more than char-only C=3.0 or may not improve spam recall. The prior majority-class collapse under word-only C=0.3 could persist if class imbalance dominates. This is a primary-split probe, not a verified improvement.

proposal.reason: Trial 3 is the strongest completed primary trial so far with word+char features at C=3.0, but it has a nonzero train/search gap and imperfect spam recall. Testing the same word+char representation at lower regularization strength C=0.3 is a reasonable primary-split probe to see whether reduced capacity improves generalization or preserves the spam recall gained over word-only C=0.3 in trial 1.
proposal.review: Primary evidence is limited to trials 1-3. Trial 1 word-only C=0.3 collapsed to majority-class behavior with spam recall 0.0. Trial 2 char-only C=3.0 improved macro_f1 to 0.9257 with spam recall 0.7692. Trial 3 word+char C=3.0 was best so far at macro_f1 0.9373 with spam recall 0.8022, but its train/search gap was 0.0546. No confirmation-split measurements are available or compared.
proposal.hypothesis: Lowering C from 3.0 to 0.3 for the word+char representation may reduce overfitting and potentially improve macro_f1 or spam recall relative to trial 3, but the direction and magnitude are unknown and the lower capacity could also weaken spam recall.
proposal.uncertainty: This is a primary-split probe, not a verified improvement. The effect of lowering C for word+char features is unknown; it may reduce the train/search gap without improving macro_f1, or it may underfit and lose spam recall. Prior word-only C=0.3 collapsed, but that does not determine behavior for the combined representation.
